power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The rapid expansion of online gambling and sports betting has raised concerns about gambling-related harm and its implications for public health.
However, nationwide evidence regarding temporal trends and patterns of health care utilization associated with gambling remains limited, particularly in low-and middle-income countries.
We conducted a nationwide retrospective study using administrative data from Brazil's Unified Health System from 2014 through 2025.
We examined primary health care records associated with pathological gambling (ICD-10, code F63.0) and gambling and betting (code Z72.6).
We analyzed temporal trends, seasonal patterns, and geographic and demographic distributions, calculating annual encounter rates per 100,000 inhabitants.
Gambling-related primary health care encounters increased substantially during the study period, with a marked acceleration beginning in 2022.
By 2025, nationwide rates reached 1.46 encounters per 100,000 inhabitants for pathological gambling and 0.60 per 100,000 for gambling and betting.
Increases were observed across all five Brazilian regions, with the highest rates in the South and Southeast.
Recorded encounters increased across age groups and both sexes, particularly among adults aged 20 to 39 years.
Rates were also elevated among adolescent males and older women.
Time-series analyses suggested seasonal variation, with higher indices generally between April and October.
Gambling-related encounters in Brazilian primary health care increased markedly from 2014 through 2025, particularly after 2022, with substantial demographic and geographic variation.

These findings indicate increasing documentation of gamblingrelated conditions within a nationwide public health system and underscore the need for improved surveillance, early identification, and access to appropriate mental health care.

Gambling disorder is an increasingly important public health concern, characterized by persistent or recurrent gambling behavior despite substantial personal, financial, and social consequences (World Health Organization (WHO), 2024).
The rapid expansion of online gambling platforms and sports betting has substantially increased the accessibility of gambling, raising concerns about its implications for mental health.

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis estimated that 46.2% of adults worldwide had participated in gambling during the preceding year, with 1.41% engaging in problematic gambling (Tran et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A recent systematic review and meta-analysis estimated that 46.2% of adults worldwide had participated in gambling during the preceding year, with 1.41% engaging in problematic gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Tran et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These findings underscore the substantial global exposure to gambling and the need to understand its health consequences, particularly in countries where digital gambling has expanded rapidly.
The clinical burden of gambling disorder extends beyond financial losses and includes considerable psychiatric morbidity, functional impairment, and increased mortality.

Gambling disorder is strongly associated with substance use, mood, and anxiety disorders, with a recent meta-analysis estimating that 82.2% of affected individuals had at least one co-occurring psychiatric disorder (Galeazzi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Gambling disorder is strongly associated with substance use, mood, and anxiety disorders, with a recent meta-analysis estimating that 82.2% of affected individuals had at least one co-occurring psychiatric disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Galeazzi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Gambling-related harms have also been associated with suicidal behavior, family disruption, financial insecurity, and socioeconomic inequalities (Wardle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Gambling-related harms have also been associated with suicidal behavior, family disruption, financial insecurity, and socioeconomic inequalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Wardle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Despite these consequences, gambling disorder remains insufficiently characterized in health care surveillance, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, where information about its clinical burden and patterns of health service utilization is limited.
Brazil provides an important setting for investigating the epidemiology of gambling disorder.
The expansion of online betting has raised public health concerns in a country marked by substantial socioeconomic and regional inequalities.

A nationally representative survey conducted in 2022-2023 found that 17.6% of individuals aged 14 years or older had participated in gambling during the preceding year, whereas 2.8% were classified as engaging in moderate-or high-risk gambling (Madruga et al., 2026)
text.formatted: A nationally representative survey conducted in 2022-2023 found that 17.6% of individuals aged 14 years or older had participated in gambling during the preceding year, whereas 2.8% were classified as engaging in moderate-or high-risk gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Madruga et al., 2026)</ref>

text.text: Time-series analysis was done through the "Forecast" package, analyzing raw outpatient visit numbers, since monthly population numbers were not available.
To calculate rates per 100,000 patient visits, we summed monthly visits within each year to accurately adjust for population, since population data are available by year.
Race/Ethnic data were normalized by the gender-specific national population, because specific racial population counts/estimates were not available for all analyzed years.
Data were analyzed using R (version 4.4.2) and RStudio (2024.04.2 Build 764), and data visualization was performed through the "geobr" and "ggplot2" packages.

For the Brazilian regional maps and age-dependent analysis, we chose 2014, 2018, 2022, and 2025 because they mark key years in Brazil's gambling legislation. 2014 marks the first year of control; 2018 is when fixed-odds betting was legalized ("LEI N o 13.756," 2018); 2022 was the deadline for betting companies to register under the law ("LEI N o 14.790," 2023); and 2025 is the latest available year with complete data under the 2025 sports-betting regulatory framework ("PORTARIA SPA/MF N o 817," 2025).

Because SIAPS serves 72% of the population and we corrected data using official government counts and estimates, we avoided statistical testing when comparing the impact of conditions across regions, sexes, races, and age groups.

Notably, men show an earlier onset, with ages 10-14 (F63.0: 0.418 and Z72.6: 0.068) and 15-19 (F63.0: 0.908 and Z72.6: 0.488) already showing increased outpatient visits, while women remain relatively low at 10-14 (F63.0: 0.418 and Z72.6: 0.021) and 15-19 (F63.0: 0.156 and Z72.6: 0.054) (Fig. 3).

text.text: From ages 20-29 (Men-F63.0: 1.749 and Z72.6: 0.867; Women-F63.0: 1.286 and Z72.6: 0.632), 30-39 (Men-F63.0: 1.420 and Z72.6: 0.691; Women-F63.0: 1.558 and Z72.6: 0.719), and 40-49 (Men-F63.0: 0.673 and Z72.6: 0.235; Women-F63.0: 0.798 and Z72.6: 0.247), both sexes show a substantial increase, representing the largest fraction of outpatient visits (Fig. 3).

text.text: Ages 50 onward show a relative reduction compared with previous age groups, but higher rates in women than in men (Fig. 3).

text.text: When analyzing outpatient visits in the racial/ethnic subset, we identified similar profiles between black and white populations regarding Pathological gambling (F63.0).
We didn't observe gender differences within either race.
In 2025, black men and women reached 0.33 and 0.36 outpatient visits per 100,000 people, respectively, while white men and women reached 0.33 and 0.23 visits per 100,000 people, respectively.

Asian and Native-American populations had markedly lower rates, with Asian men and women at 0.02 and 0.01, respectively, while Native-American men had 0 visits in 2025 and Native-American women had 0.001 (Fig. 4A).

text.text: Gambling and betting (Z72.6) show a similar trend, with the white and black populations having similarly high levels in 2025, with black men and women reaching 0.16 and 0.14 outpatient visits per 100,000 people, respectively, and white men and women reaching 0.14 and 0.11 visits.
Asian populations showed 0.007 and 0.005 outpatient visits per 100,000, and the Native American population recorded no visits during the entire period (Fig. 4B).

B) Outpatient visits for Gambling and Betting (Z72.6) by race/ethnicity and sex per 100,000 people from 2014 to 2025 in Brazil.

In this nationwide retrospective study of gambling-related primary health care encounters in Brazil, we identified an increase in records associated with pathological gambling (ICD-10 F63.0) and gambling and betting (ICD-10 Z72.6) between 2014 and 2025, particularly after 2022.
By 2025, national rates had reached 1.46 and 0.60 recorded encounters per 100,000 inhabitants, respectively.
Increases were observed across all five geographic regions and among both sexes, with particularly prominent changes among young adults.
These findings are consistent with growing concerns about gamblingrelated harm worldwide.
A systematic review and meta-analysis estimated that 46.2% of adults had gambled during the preceding year and that 1.41% experienced problematic gambling (Tran et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A systematic review and meta-analysis estimated that 46.2% of adults had gambled during the preceding year and that 1.41% experienced problematic gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Tran et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In Brazil, the Third National Alcohol and Drugs Survey (LENAD III) found that 17.6% of individuals aged 14 years or older had gambled during the preceding year, with 2.8% classified as moderate-or high-risk gamblers (Madruga et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In Brazil, the Third National Alcohol and Drugs Survey (LENAD III) found that 17.6% of individuals aged 14 years or older had gambled during the preceding year, with 2.8% classified as moderate-or high-risk gamblers <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Madruga et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although these population estimates are not directly comparable with clinical encounters, our findings document an increasing representation of gambling-related conditions in Brazilian primary health care.
The marked increase in gambling-related encounters occurred during substantial changes in the availability, accessibility, and regulation of gambling in Brazil.

The expansion of online gambling has transformed participation by enabling continuous access through mobile devices, reducing geographic barriers, and increasing opportunities for rapid, repeated betting (Ghelfi et al., 2023; Wardle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The expansion of online gambling has transformed participation by enabling continuous access through mobile devices, reducing geographic barriers, and increasing opportunities for rapid, repeated betting <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Ghelfi et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Wardle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In Brazil, fixed-odds sports betting was legalized in 2018 ("LEI N o 13.756," 2018), followed by broader regulation of online gambling in 2023 ("LEI N o 14.790," 2023) and implementation of federal authorization requirements in 2025 ("PORTARIA SPA/MF N o 817," 2025).
The temporal increase identified in our study is particularly noteworthy because it became more pronounced in 2022, before the implementation of the most recent regulatory framework.

The LENAD III survey identified online gambling as a particularly strong correlate of gambling-related risk (Tran et al., 2024), suggesting that changes in gambling accessibility may have important public health implications.
text.formatted: The LENAD III survey identified online gambling as a particularly strong correlate of gambling-related risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Tran et al., 2024)</ref>, suggesting that changes in gambling accessibility may have important public health implications.

text.text: Changes in awareness, health-seeking behavior, diagnostic practices, and the completeness of administrative records may also have contributed to the observed trends.
The increase in gambling-related primary health care encounters is particularly relevant when considered alongside the broader trajectory of psychiatric health care in Brazil.

In a recent nationwide study of the Brazilian Unified Health System, Resende et al. reported that psychiatric hospitalization rates declined by approximately 52% between 2008 and 2022 (Resende et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a recent nationwide study of the Brazilian Unified Health System, <ref type="bibr">Resende et al.</ref> reported that psychiatric hospitalization rates declined by approximately 52% between 2008 and 2022 <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Resende et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, this study identified an increase in gambling-related primary-care records, beginning particularly in the latter part of 2022 and continuing through 2025.

Although the two studies evaluated different levels of care and their observation periods overlapped only partially, these findings suggest potentially divergent patterns of mental health service utilization.

Reductions in psychiatric hospitalizations should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence of declining psychiatric morbidity, particularly for disorders that are increasingly recognized or managed in outpatient settings.
The growing documentation of gambling-related conditions may therefore represent an additional challenge for Brazil's community-based mental health services.
Despite the increase observed during the study period, the absolute rates of gambling-related primary-care encounters remained low relative to population-based estimates of gambling-related risk.
This discrepancy is consistent with previous evidence showing that many individuals experiencing gambling-related problems do not receive professional treatment.

A systematic review found that gambling disorder is rarely assessed systematically in primary care and that general practitioners frequently report insufficient knowledge, confidence, or training in its management (Tatar et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A systematic review found that gambling disorder is rarely assessed systematically in primary care and that general practitioners frequently report insufficient knowledge, confidence, or training in its management <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Tatar et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Previous research has identified stigma, limited awareness of treatment services, and reluctance to disclose gambling problems as barriers to help-seeking (Gainsbury et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Previous research has identified stigma, limited awareness of treatment services, and reluctance to disclose gambling problems as barriers to help-seeking <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Gainsbury et al., 2014</ref>).

text.text: An additional consideration is that gambling-related harms may not be recorded under gambling-specific diagnostic codes when individuals present with associated psychiatric or physical health complaints.

A recent meta-analysis estimated that 82.2% of individuals with gambling disorder had at least one co-occurring psychiatric disorder, particularly substance use, mood, and anxiety disorders (Galeazzi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis estimated that 82.2% of individuals with gambling disorder had at least one co-occurring psychiatric disorder, particularly substance use, mood, and anxiety disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Galeazzi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Gamblingrelated problems have also been associated with suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and suicide mortality (Kristensen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Gamblingrelated problems have also been associated with suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and suicide mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Kristensen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the relatively low rates identified in the present study may reflect incomplete recognition and documentation of gamblingrelated problems within routine primary care rather than a correspondingly low population burden.

Importantly, the two ICD-10 categories examined here represent different clinical constructs: F63.0 refers to pathological gambling, whereas Z72.6 records gambling and betting without necessarily indicating a psychiatric disorder (World Health Organization (WHO), 2019).
The demographic distribution of gambling-related encounters provides additional insights into populations potentially requiring targeted prevention and treatment.
By 2025, most age groups in both sexes showed increases, with particularly high rates among adults aged 20 to 39 years.
Among males, elevated rates were also recorded during adolescence, whereas women showed relatively higher rates in some older age groups.
These findings are consistent in part with recent Brazilian survey evidence.

In a nationally representative study of online betting participation, Magini et al. found that adults aged 18 to 34 years had substantially higher odds of online betting than adults aged 60 years or older, and that men had higher odds of participation than women (Magini et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a nationally representative study of online betting participation, Magini et al. found that adults aged 18 to 34 years had substantially higher odds of online betting than adults aged 60 years or older, and that men had higher odds of participation than women <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Magini et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence from a systematic review of gambling during childhood, adolescence, and emerging adulthood also identified increased vulnerability among young people, particularly males, and associations between novel gambling activities and problematic gambling (Richard and King, 2023).
text.formatted: Evidence from a systematic review of gambling during childhood, adolescence, and emerging adulthood also identified increased vulnerability among young people, particularly males, and associations between novel gambling activities and problematic gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Richard and King, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, patterns of gambling participation should not be equated with patterns of gambling-related health care utilization.
Differences in clinical recognition, help-seeking behavior, and symptom severity may contribute to the age-and sex-specific distributions we identified.
The presence of gambling-related clinical records among adolescents is particularly concerning and supports the importance of early identification and prevention.
Geographic analyses revealed increasing gambling-related encounters across all Brazilian regions, with the highest recorded rates in the South and Southeast by 2025.
These differences may reflect variations in gambling accessibility, socioeconomic conditions, digital connectivity, health care infrastructure, and the recognition of gambling-related conditions.

A systematic review examining inequalities in gamblingrelated harms found that socioeconomic status, age, education, ethnicity, and gambling behavior were associated with differences in the distribution of harm (Raybould et al., 2021).
text.formatted: A systematic review examining inequalities in gamblingrelated harms found that socioeconomic status, age, education, ethnicity, and gambling behavior were associated with differences in the distribution of harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Raybould et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, gambling-related harm extends beyond clinical diagnoses and may include financial insecurity, family conflict, psychological distress, occupational impairment, and social disadvantage (Langham et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Moreover, gambling-related harm extends beyond clinical diagnoses and may include financial insecurity, family conflict, psychological distress, occupational impairment, and social disadvantage <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Langham et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, geographic differences in recorded encounters may reflect both variations in gambling-related morbidity and inequalities in access to health care.
The lower rates documented in some regions cannot be interpreted as evidence of a lower underlying burden without accounting for differences in service availability and clinical ascertainment.
Similarly, interpret the racial and ethnic distributions observed in our study cautiously because appropriate race-specific population denominators were not available throughout the study period.
These limitations reinforce the need to strengthen epidemiological surveillance among historically underserved populations.
The time-series analyses also suggested seasonal variation in gambling-related encounters, with higher seasonal indices generally observed between April and October.
This pattern may partly reflect the Brazilian football calendar, which provides sustained opportunities for sports betting throughout much of the year.

State football championships traditionally begin in January, while the Brazilian National Championship (Campeonato Brasileiro Série A) generally begins in March or April and runs through the final months of the year.
In 2025, for example, state championships began in January, and the national championship started on March 29 ((CBF), 2024).
The shift from regional competitions to a longer national football season could contribute to sustained betting exposure during the middle and latter portions of the year.
Nevertheless, this interpretation remains speculative.
The available data do not identify individual gambling activities, betting frequency, or the temporal relationship between gambling exposure and clinical encounters.
Seasonal variation in financial circumstances, help-seeking behavior, and health service utilization may also contribute to the observed patterns.
Studies integrating gambling activity, sporting calendars, and clinical data are needed to investigate these associations.
The increasing documentation of gambling-related conditions has important implications for mental health policy and primary-care practice in Brazil.

Gambling disorder is associated with substantial psychiatric morbidity (Galeazzi et al., 2025), and suicidal behavior represents an important clinical concern among affected individuals (Kristensen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Gambling disorder is associated with substantial psychiatric morbidity <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Galeazzi et al., 2025)</ref>, and suicidal behavior represents an important clinical concern among affected individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Kristensen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: International clinical guidelines recommend the identification of gambling-related harm, assessment of psychiatric comorbidities and suicide risk, and the establishment of referral pathways to specialized treatment when appropriate ((NICE), 2025).

Primary health care may represent an important setting for these interventions, particularly because patients experiencing gambling-related problems may initially present with anxiety, depression, substance use, or financial and interpersonal difficulties.
The integration of gambling-related assessment into routine mental health care, professional training, and community-based referral services could improve clinical recognition.

At the population level, prevention strategies should also address environmental and commercial determinants of gambling-related harm, including advertising, accessibility, and product design (Wardle et al., 2024).
text.formatted: At the population level, prevention strategies should also address environmental and commercial determinants of gambling-related harm, including advertising, accessibility, and product design <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Wardle et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These measures may be especially relevant in Brazil, where the rapid expansion of digital gambling has occurred alongside persistent socioeconomic and geographic inequalities.
Our study has several limitations.
First, we used aggregated administrative data that did not include individual clinical histories, validated diagnostic assessments, or information regarding gambling severity and duration.

Second, the records represent documented primary-care encounters rather than all individuals experiencing gamblingrelated harm, and therefore cannot establish the incidence or prevalence of gambling disorder.
Third, although the data identify unique individuals within each month, the same person may appear in multiple months, preventing the estimation of annual uniquepatient counts.

Fourth, the lack of individual-level information on gambling modalities, socioeconomic circumstances, psychiatric comorbidities, and treatment limited the interpretation of demographic and geographic differences.
Finally, the descriptive design does not permit causal attribution of changes in health care utilization to gambling market expansion, regulatory developments, or specific sporting events.

In conclusion, gambling-related primary health care encounters increased substantially in Brazil between 2014 and 2025, particularly after 2022, with considerable demographic, geographic, and seasonal heterogeneity.
This increase occurred against a historical background of declining psychiatric hospitalizations nationwide, highlighting the evolving demands placed on Brazil's mental health system.

Although the findings cannot establish changes in the population prevalence of gambling disorder, they document increasing clinical recognition or recording of gambling-related conditions within the public primary-care system.

Strengthening surveillance, integrating gamblingrelated assessment into mental health services, and expanding equitable access to prevention and treatment may help address the emerging public health challenges associated with gambling. discussions and your assistance during times of urgency.

Although these findings indicate substantial exposure to gambling-related harm, population surveys cannot establish the extent to which these problems are recognized, diagnosed, and treated within the health care system.

Brazil's Unified Health System (Sistema Único de Saúde, SUS) provides publicly funded mental health services through primary care, specialized psychosocial care centers, and hospitals, offering an opportunity to examine the recorded clinical burden of gambling disorder across a large and geographically diverse population (Ministério da Saúde, 2026).

Nationwide health care records can complement population surveys by identifying temporal changes in diagnosed disorders, patterns of service utilization, and demographic and geographic differences in access to care.
However, the extent to which gambling disorder is represented in routine health care data, and how this representation has changed over time, remains inadequately understood.
Such information is essential for assessing health system responses, identifying potentially underserved populations, and guiding resource allocation and prevention strategies.

In this nationwide epidemiological study, we used administrative data from the SUS to examine temporal trends and demographic and geographic patterns in health care encounters recorded with gambling disorder in Brazil.

Methods Data collection All data used in this study were obtained from the Primary Health Care Information System of the Brazilian Unified Health System (SIAPS/SUS) managed by the Secretariat of Primary Health Care (SAPS).

We selected the two most prominent conditions associated with gambling habits classified by the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10): Pathological gambling (F63.0) and Gambling and betting (Z72.6).
We selected the following interest variables: Age group, Sex, Race/ethnicity, Geographical region, and ICD-10 code; and the parameter: number of outpatient visits.

Because we could not download data for each analysis as a single dataset, we organized the data into separate datasets: national, regional, and time-series analyses shared a single dataset, whereas age-group, race/ethnicity, and educational attainment analyses each used a separate dataset.

The database comprises consolidated information sent by primary healthcare units, consisting of anonymized clinical assessments documented in primary health care, and should not be interpreted as definitive diagnoses established through specialized psychological or psychiatric evaluation.
Data were retrieved from 2014 to 2025 by month/year of the patient visit and reflect the number of unique patients each month to reduce repeated patient visits.
Public primary health care served 72% of the Brazilian population in 2024 (https://bvsms.saude.gov.br/bvs/publicacoes/relatorio_anual_gestao_2024.pdf), representing a large share of the population.
We do not have access to any individual patient data or information, only aggregate population-level data.
Regional divisions are valid and represent official administrative divisions proposed by the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística-IBGE).
We obtained population data from IBGE censuses and estimates throughout the analysis and used them to calculate rates per 100,000.
